title: In Isaiah 36 What Lessons Can We Learn From The Way The Assyrians Approached Their Enemies Particularly In Terms Of Spiritual Warfare
paragraphs: Historical Context: Isaiah 36 and the Threat of Assyria

Isaiah 36 records the dramatic moment when the mighty Assyrian empire, under King Sennacherib, besieges Jerusalem. The Assyrian field commander, known as the Rabshakeh, stands before the city’s walls and addresses King Hezekiah’s officials—and, by extension, the people of Judah—with a mixture of intimidation, mockery, and psychological warfare.

This chapter is more than a historical account; it offers profound lessons on spiritual warfare, showing how the enemies of God’s people often use similar tactics to unsettle, discourage, and tempt believers to distrust the Lord.
Assyrian Tactics: Psychological Warfare and Spiritual Implications
1. The Use of Fear and Intimidation
The Rabshakeh repeatedly emphasizes the might of Assyria, reminding Judah of the futility of resistance:

Now, behold, thou trustest upon the staff of this bruised reed, even upon Egypt; whereon if a man lean, it will go into his hand, and pierce it: so is Pharaoh king of Egypt to all that trust on him. - Isaiah 36:6 ASV

The enemy delights in sowing doubt about the reliability of human alliances and resources. In spiritual warfare, Satan often highlights our vulnerability and weaknesses, tempting us to despair or look for help apart from God.
2. Undermining Faith in God’s Promises
The Rabshakeh openly questions God’s ability to deliver Judah:

But if thou say unto me, We trust in Jehovah our God: is not that he, whose high places and whose altars Hezekiah hath taken away... therefore give pledges, I pray thee, to my master the king of Assyria... - Isaiah 36:7 ASV

He misrepresents true worship and mocks the reforms Hezekiah implemented. Likewise, in spiritual warfare, Satan twists God’s Word and attempts to shake our confidence in the sufficiency of Christ and the reliability of God’s promises (Genesis 3:1 ASV; Matthew 4:3 ASV).
3. Offering False Alternatives and Empty Promises
The Rabshakeh offers the people of Jerusalem a deal if they surrender:

Make an agreement with me by a present, and come out to me; and eat ye every one of his vine, and every one of his fig-tree, and drink ye every one the waters of his own cistern; until I come and take you away to a land like your own land... - Isaiah 36:16-17 ASV
He promises comfort and security in exchange for their surrender, echoing how the enemy often entices believers with short-term “solutions” that ultimately lead to spiritual bondage.
4. Public Pressure and Discouragement
The Assyrian spokesman deliberately speaks in Hebrew, so that all the people on the wall can understand and be demoralized:
But the Rabshakeh said... Hath my master sent me to thy master and to thee to speak these words? Hath he not sent me to the men that sit upon the wall...? - Isaiah 36:12 ASV
In spiritual warfare, discouragement is often spread publicly, seeking to create a climate of fear and hopelessness. The enemy targets not only leaders but the whole community of faith.
Lessons for Spiritual Warfare Today

Stand Firm in God’s Word: When confronted by lies, intimidation, and distorted truths, believers must cling to the promises of God. The authority and sufficiency of Scripture is our shield (Ephesians 6:17 ASV).

Don’t Negotiate with the Enemy: The people of Jerusalem did not respond to the Rabshakeh’s offers. Instead, they remained silent and brought their concerns to God through Hezekiah and Isaiah (Isaiah 37:1 ASV). In our battles, we turn to prayer and spiritual counsel, not compromise.

Trust in God’s Power, Not Human Strength: The Assyrians trusted in their military might, but God delivers those who trust in Him alone (Psalm 20:7 ASV). Salvation is by grace through faith, not by human effort (Ephesians 2:8-9 ASV).
Recognize the Enemy’s Strategy: The tactics of confusion, fear, and false promises are still used today. We are called to be alert and to resist the devil, firm in our faith (1 Peter 5:8-9 ASV).
Christ-Centered Application

Ultimately, all spiritual warfare points us to the victory of Christ. Jesus faced the full force of the enemy’s accusations and temptations, yet overcame by relying on God’s Word and fulfilling God’s plan (Hebrews 4:15 ASV). Because of His triumph, we too can stand firm, knowing that "greater is he that is in you than he that is in the world" (1 John 4:4 ASV).
Conclusion

Isaiah 36 is a timeless reminder of the schemes of the enemy and the sufficiency of God. As we face our own spiritual battles, let us learn from the people of Judah—not to be intimidated or deceived, but to trust wholly in the Lord, seeking His deliverance and standing firm in His truth.
